source: 90% of girls vaccinated against HPV by age 15

claim: The local need for and impact of cervical cancer preventive measures depend on the burden in a given population, which is determined by context-specific sexual behaviour, and HPV prevalence.
source: The local need for and impact of cervical cancer preventive measures depend on the burden in a given population, which is determined by context-specific sexual behaviour, and HPV prevalence (Guan et al., 2012).

claim: Impact projections of cervical cancer preventive measures can help local health authorities set adequate public health targets and allocate resources accordingly when based on adequate data.
source: When based on adequate data, impact projections of cervical cancer preventive measures can help local health authorities set adequate public health targets and allocate resources accordingly (Goldie et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goldie et al., 2006

claim: High-quality type- and age-specific data on HPV prevalence and cervical cancer incidence from local populations are often unavailable.
source: High-quality type- and age-specific data on HPV prevalence and cervical cancer incidence from local populations are often unavailable.
evidence: General statement about data availability challenges

claim: Data on sexual behaviour, such as sex outside marriage, are prone to bias including social desirability and recall bias.
source: The same holds for adequate data on sexual behaviour, for example, data on sex outside marriage, which are also prone to bias, for example, social desirability and recall bias (Morris et al., 2014; Kelly et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morris et al., 2014 and Kelly et al., 2013

claim: India is the country with the world's highest expected burden of cervical cancer.
source: The framework is presented using a case study in India, the country with the world's highest expected burden of cervical cancer (Bonjour et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bonjour et al., 2021

claim: India has very limited access to cervical cancer preventive measures.
source: the country with the world's highest expected burden of cervical cancer (Bonjour et al., 2021) and very limited access to cervical cancer preventive measures (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sankaranarayanan et al., 2019

claim: There were two Indian states (out of 25 states or groups of states) with high-quality type- and age-specific HPV prevalence data needed for impact projections.

evidence: Supported by citations to Franceschi et al., 2005; Dutta et al., 2012; Kataria et al., 2022

claim: There were 12 Indian states with cervical cancer incidence and sexual behaviour data.
source: In the Indian case study, there were 12 states with cervical cancer incidence (Bray et al., 2017; Report of National Cancer Registry Programme, 2020) and sexual behaviour data, which were assigned to the intermediate level of data availability.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bray et al., 2017 and Report of National Cancer Registry Programme, 2020

claim: There were 11 Indian states that only had data on sexual behaviour.
source: The remaining 11 states only had data on sexual behaviour (National Behavioural Surveillance Survey: General Population, 2006) and were assigned to the low level of data availability.
evidence: Supported by citation to National Behavioural Surveillance Survey: General Population, 2006

claim: Model fit improved substantially when increasing the number of prefixed clusters from two to three, with the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) reducing from 6933 to 5700.
source: Model fit improved substantially when increasing the number of prefixed clusters from two to three, with the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) reducing from 6933 to 5700 (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1

claim: Further increases in the number of prefixed clusters to four only led to marginal improvement in model fit, with a small reduction in BIC from 5700 to 5532.
source: Further increases in the number of prefixed clusters to four only led to marginal improvement in model fit, with a small reduction in BIC from 5700 to 5532
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1

claim: With the number of prefixed clusters set at five, the clustering method no longer converged.
source: With the number of prefixed clusters set at five, the clustering method no longer converged.
evidence: Direct statement about clustering method performance

claim: Two or three clusters were fitting to describe the patterns of cervical cancer incidence in the available data.
source: We concluded that two or three clusters were fitting to describe the patterns of cervical cancer incidence in the available data.
evidence: Conclusion based on BIC analysis

claim: In the 2-clustering, cluster 1 had a low maximum incidence of 47 cases per 100,000 women-years at age group 60–64 years.
source: When allowing two clusters, cluster 1 had a low maximum incidence of 47 cases per 100,000 women-years at age group 60–64 years
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 2

claim: In the 2-clustering, cluster 2 had a higher maximum incidence of 91 cases per 100,000 women-years at the earlier age group of 55–59 years.
source: compared to cluster 2 with its higher maximum incidence of 91 cases per 100,000 women-years at the earlier age group of 55–59 years (Figure 2, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 2

claim: In the 3-clustering, an additional cluster was characterized by intermediate maximum incidence of 64 cases per 100,000 women-years at age group 60–64 years.
source: When allowing three clusters, we observed an additional cluster characterized by intermediate maximum incidence of 64 cases per 100,000 women-years at age group 60–64 years (Figure 2, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 2

claim: The variable with the highest predictive value for cluster of cervical cancer incidence patterns was 'proportion of urban male respondents reporting sex with non-regular partners in the last 12 months'.
source: The variables with the first, second, and third highest predictive values for cluster of cervical cancer incidence patterns were 'proportion of urban male respondents reporting sex with non-regular partners in the last 12 months', 'median age of first sex in rural males', and 'median age of first sex in urban females', respectively (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—source data 2

claim: The variable with the second highest predictive value for cluster of cervical cancer incidence patterns was 'median age of first sex in rural males'.
source: The variables with the first, second, and third highest predictive values for cluster of cervical cancer incidence patterns were 'proportion of urban male respondents reporting sex with non-regular partners in the last 12 months', 'median age of first sex in rural males', and 'median age of first sex in urban females', respectively (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—source data 2

claim: The variable with the third highest predictive value for cluster of cervical cancer incidence patterns was 'median age of first sex in urban females'.
source: The variables with the first, second, and third highest predictive values for cluster of cervical cancer incidence patterns were 'proportion of urban male respondents reporting sex with non-regular partners in the last 12 months', 'median age of first sex in rural males', and 'median age of first sex in urban females', respectively (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 3—source data 2

claim: High proportions of urban male respondents reporting sex with non-regular partners in the last 12 months were associated with the high-incidence cluster.
source: In particular, there was a good distinction between the high- and low-incidence clusters in terms of 'proportion of urban male respondents reporting sex with non-regular partners in the last 12 months', with high proportions associated with the high-incidence cluster (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3

claim: High values of 'median age of first sex in females' were associated with the high-incidence cluster.
source: High values of 'median age of first sex in females' and low values of 'median age of first age in males' were also associated for the high-incidence cluster, although the distinction was less clear.
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: Low values of 'median age of first sex in males' were associated with the high-incidence cluster.
source: High values of 'median age of first sex in females' and low values of 'median age of first age in males' were also associated for the high-incidence cluster, although the distinction was less clear.
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: The estimated out-of-bag error of the constructed classifier was 29%.
source: The estimated out-of-bag error of the constructed classifier was 29%.
evidence: Direct statement of classifier performance metric

claim: When applying the constructed classifier to the Indian states with identified clusters, only Karnataka and other North Eastern states (2 of 14 states; 14%) were wrongly classified to the low-incidence cluster.
source: When applying the constructed classifier to the Indian states with identified clusters, only Karnataka and other North Eastern states (2 of 14 states; 14%) were wrongly classified to the low-incidence cluster (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 3

claim: All 11 remaining Indian states received a higher probability of belonging to the low-incidence cluster.
source: All 11 remaining Indian states received a higher probability of belonging to the low-incidence cluster (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 3

claim: In total, 19 and 6 states were identified for the low- and high-incidence clusters, respectively.
source: Hence, we identified in total 19 and 6 states for the low- and high-incidence clusters, respectively.
evidence: Summary of classification results

claim: The HPV prevalence reported by the survey corresponding to the high-incidence cluster was 16.9% in women in the age range 20–60 years.
source: We verified that the HPV prevalence reported by the survey corresponding to the high-incidence cluster was higher than the prevalence reported by the one corresponding to the low-incidence cluster: HPV prevalence of 16.9% vs 9.8% (in women in the age range 20–60 years).
evidence: Supported by data from surveys cited earlier (Franceschi et al., 2005; Dutta et al., 2012)

claim: The HPV prevalence reported by the survey corresponding to the low-incidence cluster was 9.8% in women in the age range 20–60 years.
source: We verified that the HPV prevalence reported by the survey corresponding to the high-incidence cluster was higher than the prevalence reported by the one corresponding to the low-incidence cluster: HPV prevalence of 16.9% vs 9.8% (in women in the age range 20–60 years).
evidence: Supported by data from surveys cited earlier (Franceschi et al., 2005; Dutta et al., 2012)

claim: There was a 1.7-fold difference in HPV prevalence between the high-incidence and low-incidence clusters.
source: This 1.7-fold difference in HPV prevalence was in the same order of magnitude as the 1.9-fold difference we found for the age-standardized cervical cancer incidence between the two clusters (17.9 vs 9.01 cases per 100,000 women-years).
evidence: Calculated from HPV prevalence data

claim: There was a 1.9-fold difference in age-standardized cervical cancer incidence between the high-incidence and low-incidence clusters (17.9 vs 9.01 cases per 100,000 women-years).
source: This 1.7-fold difference in HPV prevalence was in the same order of magnitude as the 1.9-fold difference we found for the age-standardized cervical cancer incidence between the two clusters (17.9 vs 9.01 cases per 100,000 women-years).
evidence: Calculated from cervical cancer incidence data

claim: India can be divided into two main groups of 19 and 6 Indian states or groups of states that are characterized by low or high cervical cancer incidence, respectively.
source: We found that India can be divided into two main groups of 19 and 6 Indian states or groups of states that are characterized by low or high cervical cancer incidence, respectively.
evidence: Summary of clustering and classification results

claim: Individuals, in particular men, in high-incidence states had more sexual activity with non-regular partners, including commercial partners, than in low-incidence states.
source: As expected, and in line with previous studies, individuals, in particular men, in high-incidence states had more sexual activity with non-regular partners, including commercial partners, than in low-incidence states (Vaccarella et al., 2006; Schulte-Frohlinde et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by data analysis and citations to Vaccarella et al., 2006 and Schulte-Frohlinde et al., 2022

claim: Early sexual debut in women has previously been suggested to be associated with high cervical cancer incidence and HPV positivity.
source: While early sexual debut in women has also previously been suggested to be associated with high cervical cancer incidence and HPV positivity (Vaccarella et al., 2006; Schulte-Frohlinde et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Vaccarella et al., 2006 and Schulte-Frohlinde et al., 2022

claim: In the Indian dataset, early sexual debut was associated with lower cervical cancer incidence.
source: it was associated with lower cervical cancer incidence in the dataset we considered.
evidence: Based on data analysis in this study

claim: For the Indian context, early sexual debut is common in states with a larger rural population, among whom less sexual activity occurs with non-regular partners.
source: We hypothesize that, for the Indian context, early sexual debut is common in states with a larger rural population, among whom less sexual activity occurs with non-regular partners, which is the main determining factor for a lower risk of cervical cancer.
evidence: Hypothesis based on data patterns observed

claim: With the urbanization of rural areas, it is possible that more Indian states may shift to a high cancer incidence pattern, with an accompanying early peak in incidence.
source: With the urbanization of rural areas, which often entails evolving socio-cultural norms, it is possible that more Indian states may shift to a high cancer incidence pattern, with an accompanying early peak in incidence (Baussano et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to Baussano et al., 2016

claim: The Footprinting framework can approximate missing data on sexual behaviour, HPV prevalence, or cervical cancer incidence.
source: We developed a framework, hereafter named Footprinting, to approximate missing data on sexual behaviour, human papillomavirus (HPV) prevalence, or cervical cancer incidence, and applied it to an Indian case study.
evidence: Description of the framework's capabilities

claim: Two main patterns of cervical cancer incidence, characterized by high and low incidence, were identified in India.
source: Two main patterns of cervical cancer incidence, characterized by high and low incidence, were identified.
evidence: Summary of clustering results

claim: All Indian states with missing data on cervical cancer incidence were classified to the low-incidence cluster based on patterns in sexual behaviour data.
source: Based on the patterns in the sexual behaviour data, all Indian states with missing data on cervical cancer incidence were classified to the low-incidence cluster.
evidence: Summary of classification results

claim: Missing data on cervical cancer incidence and HPV prevalence were approximated based on the mean of the available data within each cluster.
source: Finally, missing data on cervical cancer incidence and HPV prevalence were approximated based on the mean of the available data within each cluster.
evidence: Description of approximation method

claim: The Footprinting framework enabled context-specific impact projections for cervical cancer preventive measures to assist public health decisions on cervical cancer prevention in India.
source: With the Footprinting framework, we approximated missing cervical cancer epidemiological data and made context-specific impact projections for cervical cancer preventive measures, to assist public health decisions on cervical cancer prevention in India and other countries.
evidence: Summary of framework application and outcomes

claim: Cervical cancer incidence data were extracted from volume XI of Cancer Incidence in Five Continents (CI5).
source: The primary source of cervical cancer incidence data, which was used as Pattern data in the Clustering step, was cancer registry data from volume XI of Cancer Incidence in Five Continents (CI5) (Bray et al., 2017).
evidence: Description of data source with citation

claim: CI5 comprised incidence data from 16 cancer registries in 10 of the 25 Indian states.
source: It comprised incidence data from 16 cancer registries in 10 of the 25 Indian states (some states had more than one registry).
evidence: Description of data coverage from CI5

claim: Cervical cancer incidence data were extracted from the 2012–2016 report by the Indian National Centre for Disease Informatics and Research (NCDIR) to provide data from 17 additional cancer registries not included in CI5.
source: In addition, cervical cancer incidence data were extracted from the 2012–2016 report by the Indian National Centre for Disease Informatics and Research (NCDIR) to provide data from 17 additional cancer registries not included in CI5 (Report of National Cancer Registry Programme, 2020).
evidence: Description of additional data source with citation

claim: Combining CI5 and NCDIR sources provided incidence data for 33 registries in 14 Indian states.
source: Combining the two sources provided incidence data for 33 registries in 14 Indian states.
evidence: Summary of combined data coverage

claim: Sexual behaviour data were from the report of the National Behaviour Surveillance Survey by the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO) of India in 2006.
source: Sexual behaviour data, which were used as Footprint data in the Classification step, were from the report of the National Behaviour Surveillance Survey by the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO) of India in 2006, which was the most recent edition at the moment of writing (National Behavioural Surveillance Survey: General Population, 2006).
evidence: Description of data source with citation

claim: Sexual behaviour data for all 25 Indian states were available in the NACO survey.
source: Data for all 25 Indian states were available in the survey.
evidence: Description of data coverage

claim: The Footprinting framework is similar to other extrapolation approaches previously used in model-based projection studies targeting large geographical areas with missing data.
source: It should be noted that our Footprinting framework is similar to other extrapolation approaches previously used in model-based projection studies targeting large geographical areas with missing data, for example, a collection of LMICs or European countries (Brisson et al., 2020; Qendri et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison with existing methods supported by citations

claim: The Footprinting framework relies on the observed patterns of epidemiology in the data to select key geographical units from which impact projections are extrapolated to other units instead of working with a predefined selection of key units.
source: A strength of our framework is that it relies on the observed patterns of epidemiology in the data to select key geographical units from which impact projections are extrapolated to other units instead of working with a predefined selection of key units.
evidence: Description of framework methodology

claim: The clustering method used is able to assess the similarities between cervical cancer incidence of different geographical units based on the entire age-specific pattern.
source: Secondly, we used a newly developed clustering method (Subtil et al., 2017; Klich et al., 2021) that is able to assess the similarities between cervical cancer incidence of different geographical units based on the entire age-specific pattern, instead of clustering by age-standardized cervical cancer incidence or cervical cancer incidence in a certain age group only.
evidence: Description of clustering method with citations

claim: The nationwide estimate of cervical cancer incidence derived from aggregating the state-specific estimates was lower than the estimate reported by GLOBOCAN.
source: Furthermore, our nationwide estimate of cervical cancer incidence derived from aggregating the state-specific estimates (reported in a separate manuscript; Man et al., 2022) was lower than the estimate reported by GLOBOCAN.
evidence: Comparison of estimates with reference to separate manuscript

claim: The difference between the study's nationwide estimate and GLOBOCAN could be explained by the use of different methods of extrapolation and the inclusion of data from 17 additional cancer registries with relatively low incidence not included in GLOBOCAN estimates.
source: This could be explained by the use of different methods of extrapolation and the fact that we included data from 17 additional cancer registries with relatively low incidence not included in GLOBOCAN estimates.
evidence: Explanation based on methodological differences

claim: The Footprinting framework can be used to approximate missing economic data (e.g. treatment or vaccine delivery costs) needed to assess the health economic impact of cervical cancer preventive measures.
source: Secondly, while we focused on epidemiological data for cervical cancer, Footprinting could be used to approximate missing economic data (e.g. treatment or vaccine delivery costs) that are needed to assess the health economic impact of cervical cancer preventive measures, given that relevant Footprint data can be defined and collected.
evidence: Discussion of potential framework applications

claim: The applicability of the proposed framework depends on the amount of data available.
source: It is important to note that, in general, the applicability the proposed framework depends on the amount of data available.
evidence: Statement about framework limitations

claim: The Footprinting framework is sufficiently flexible to effectively address missing data in many situations.
source: By allowing possible adaptations, we believe that our framework is sufficiently flexible to effectively address missing data in many situations.
evidence: Statement about framework capabilities

claim: Impact projections derived using the Footprinting framework can assist local health authorities to plan and implement cervical cancer preventive strategies that are adapted to local needs and resources.
source: Such projections can assist local health authorities to plan and implement cervical cancer preventive strategies that are adapted to local needs and resources, intensifying efforts to reduce the high burden of cervical cancer still existing in many countries in low-resource settings.
evidence: Statement about practical applications of the framework

claim: The Footprinting framework enabled impact projections of cervical cancer preventive measures for the whole of India with state-specific granularity for the first time.
source: With the framework, we have derived, for the first time, impact projections of cervical cancer preventive measures for the whole of India with state-specific granularity (de Carvalho et al., 2023; Man et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about novel contribution with citations to related work

claim: Cervical cancer is an important source of disease burden worldwide.
source: Cervical cancer is an important source of disease burden worldwide (de Martel et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Martel et al., 2017

claim: The Poisson regression model for each cluster was characterized by three parameters: an intercept, one parameter for age, and one for the square of age.
source: The Poisson regression model for each cluster was characterized by three parameters: an intercept, one parameter for age, and one for the square of age.
evidence: Description of statistical model

claim: The parametric form of the Poisson regression model was chosen to match the general pattern of incidence by age, namely, increasing from zero incidence from the youngest age group, then decreasing after reaching the maximum incidence.
source: This parametric form was chosen to match the general pattern of incidence by age, namely, increasing from zero incidence from the youngest age group, then decreasing after reaching the maximum incidence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Explanation of model choice with reference to figure

claim: Classification was performed using the R package party version 1.3–7.
source: Classification was performed using the R package party version 1.3–7 with the following setting: cforest_control(teststat = 'quad', testtype = 'Univariate', mincriterion = 0.9, ntree = 50 000,, mtry = 3, maxdepth = 2, minsplit = 0, minbucket = 0).
evidence: Description of computational methods
